I take my refuge; in God, the beginningless, endless,
effulgent, cause of the world, whose will ever comes true, and
whose body consists of eternal consciousness.
Salutation to the blessed Purushottama, whose essence is
pure knowledge, and who has shaken off all bondage,—to Him,
stainless and without a second, whom only those see who have
their minds centred in deep meditation and whose wanderings
(iu the cycle of metempyphosis) have come to an end !
At the commencement of the work, the Author offers
a salutation to his Deity; as also to the original founder of the
system of philosophy, by moans of the first half of the gloka—
*Pranamya &c.' It is a usage common among people that
before beginning any action due obeisance is offered to the
Deity and to oneVT-eacbers. The effect of such obeisance lies

in the removal of obstacles in the way of the due accomplishment
of the desired work. It could not be absolutely fruitless; as in that
case, no intelligent person could ever have recourse to it. Nor
could it have any other result save the due accomplishment
of the contemplated work; as iu that case it would not necessarily be used at the commencement of that work. Then too,
in as much as what is uppermost in the person's mind at the
time that he takes up a work is the due accomplishment of that
work there is no other result approximate enough to be
accepted as following from the salutation in question..
Objection:—u Does the removal of obstacles result from
"salutation only, or from something else also ? There is no
"such necessary rule as that it follows from salutation only;
"because, t?ven in the absence of such salutation, we find two
"such Bkashyas, as that ort the N'ydya and the Mvmäasd ezhtras
"in their complete forms. Then* again, if it resulted from other
"things also, then there would be. no reasonable ground for a
"necessary recourse to this particular course only."
To the above we make the following reply :—The cessation
of obstacles results from salutation oniy; as we find all good men
having recourse to it, at the commencement of all actions. Nor
is it a fact that the authors of the Nyäya and the 3Jlm.änsä
Bhä8hyas did not offer any salutation; because they too must
have done it.
Question :—" How do you know that ?"
Answer:—We infer it from the fact of the authors
being good aod wise persons. Let the case of the wise rest;
even among the Mlcechas we find that they do not engage
themselves in any action unless they have saluted their own
divinities. Under the circumstances, it cannot be for a
moment believed, that two such extremely good and godly
persons, as Pakshila Svämi (the author of the Nyäyabhäshya)
and Qavara Svämi (the author of the Mlmänsabhäshya),
should not have offered due salutation

Page 2.] We now proceed to explain the words of the text:
" Pranamya"—the prefix 'pra denoting intensity, the word
'pranamya* denotes such salutation as is accompanied by intense
devotion and confidence; as it is such a salutation alone which,
creating a merit, destroys the very seed (possibility) of obstacles.
It is for this reason that in the case of such works as K*dambar%
and the like, we find that they were left incomplete, even
though salutation had been offered at the beginning; and the reason for this lay in the fact of the salutation in these cases nothaving
been offered with due faith and devotion,—the absence whereof
is inferred from this very fact of the works being left incomplete.
In the present case, the salutation, though being done at
the 'present time, is yet, in reality, meant to precede the composition of the Padärtkadharmasatigrakz; andjt is for this reason
that we have the sequential affix 'ktva' (in'pranamya') ; but
this affix is used only with a view to establish a syntactical
relationship between the two ( the salutation and the composition), and not merely for the purpose of indicating the said
sequence; as there would be no useful purpose served by such
indication.
' Hetum'—by means of this word * hetu' without any qualifications, the author poiuts to the fact of God being the cause of
all created things.
* fgvaram'—this word denotes a particular deity ; as it is
only in this sense that the word is used in ordinary parlance ;
and this system of philosophy is meant to be a mere compilation of things ordinarily known to men.
* Munvm!—denotes a particular person of austere pennance,
who has had the darkness of ignorance destroyed by the pure _
knowledge of Self, and who is possessed of a complete knowledge
of the whole truth regarding all things; as it is only in this seose
that this word is generally found to be used.

' Padarthadharma &c.'—' Paddrthas' are the six categories,
Substance and the rest; the *dharmas' are the common and

Pravakshyate'—-the promise of the author is that he will
propound an excellent work which will briefly explain the properties of the categories. The excellence of the work lies in
this, that the properties of things which in other works, are explained very extensively and at random, are, here, explained
briefly and in one place; this is the motive that hns led the

Obj. " A collected treatment of the properties of things is
"the cause of the due knowledge of these properties; but such
"knowledge cannot be the desired end of mac ; as the sole end of
"man lies either in the obtaining of pleasure or in the avoiding
"of pain. Consequently the work not accomplishing any desire
"of man, cannot be a fit object for acquiring".
In reply to this we have the word 'mahodayah' which
indicates the fact of the work effecting the desired end of man.
The word means—that toork from, which results the highest result, in the shape of Deliverance. This also implies that the work
bears to the Properties, the relationship of the Denoter and the
Denoted, and to the Highest Result, that of the Cause and Effect.
Question: " Well, what is this highest result ?"
In answer to this, (1) some people (the Bauddas) declare it to
be the cessation of all knowledge along with all impressions,
tendencies and longings. But this is not correct; because no
intelligent person could ever act towards the total destruction
of the self which is the dearest of all things; also because the
word 'mukti, (Deliverance), which is synonymous with the
destruction of bondage, does not mean the said cessation or
destruction.
6

(2) Others (the Vedäntis) explain it as the appearance of
pure knowledge free from all objective taint, following on the
destruction of all impressions &c This too is not right; as this
could not be possible in the absence of an efficient cause. The
cause of such knowledge consists in an augmentation of Retentiveness; and the nature of this is .such that, in the absence of
a permanent substratum, it cannot produce any particular effect;
and it at every moment, it were to appear as something new, then,
in as much as it would be undergoing a total destruction at every
moment, like the practice of leaping, it could not have gained
in power; and as such it could not be able to produce any clear
cognition; and hence there would be no possibility of such a

cognition ; specially as of the conditions of the mind as tainted
(by objectivity), the inborn capability of producing homogenous,
or like, effects aod the incapability of producing unlike ones, could
never be sec aside. Then again, in as much as ail the previous
states of the mind are naturally evanescent, the state that is herein
spoken of would be something quite different from these. Nor
is there any such single ' series ' wherein both of these could
exist; and yet Bondage and Deliverance both belong to one and
the same substratum; and these two, according to you, would refer
to two distinct objects, while, as a matter of fact, that state of
mind which cases is the same that has been functioning before.
(3) Others (the Sänkhyas) hold that after the difference between Matter and Spirit has been duly perceived, the functioning
of Matter ceases, and the Spirit rests in Its own nature; and it is
this that is Deliverance. This also is not correct; because Matter,
beiug by its very nature active, could never rest idle (indifferent,
without functioning). It might be argued that—' the functioning of Matter is caused by the purpose of the Spirit; and this
purpose being none other tjian the perception of the said difference,
as soon as this perception appears, Matter, having accomplished
its purpose, would cease to function." But this could not be ;
• as Matter being un-iotelligent, could not function with any such
discrimination (as would be necessary in accordance with the
Sänkhya theory). In fact, we find that even when it has duly
brought about a certain perception,—of sound, for instance—, it
still goes on functioning towards the same perception ; and in the
same way, even after it will have brought about discriminative
knowledge, it would go on with its functioning towards the same
end; as its active nature will not have been set aside (by the
said knowledge.}
(4) Others (the Yogis) again hold Deliverance to consist in
an experience of ever-lasting and unsurpassed pleasure. But
this view also has nothing to recommend itself; as we shall show
later on.

(5) For these reasons, we conclude that the "highest
result M consists in the absolute cessation of pain.
Question : " What is the proof of the existence of this cessation of pain*"
In reply to this, the Naiyayikas put forward the following
syllogism: 'The series of pain, being something qualified, is destroyed absolutely, because it is a series,—just like the seriesof ligiit
rays emitted l>y the lamp.' But this is not satisfactory; as the
argument is directly contradicted by the case of the series of the
colour &c. of tho atom of earth and other substances ( which
are never destroyed). Therefore we maintain that the proof of
the said cessation lies in such Upaniskat texts as 'Him without
a body, pleasure and pain do not touch.'
Objection:—"All these Upanishat passages refering merely to
the natural state of things cannot have any evidential authority."
Reply :—Not so ; as the same might be said against the
authority of Sense-perception (which also pertains to the natural
state of things).
Obj.: "What we mean, is that sentences describing the
natural state of things would be merely descriptive, and as such
devoid of evidential authority ; because these would depend upon
the authority of something else ; as such a description in itself
could never be the efficient means of any correct cognition."
Rep:—A passage cannot be regarded as descriptive simply
because it speaks of things in their fully accomplished states;
as in that case even Sense-perception would have to be regarded
as merely descriptive. In fact it is only when it speaks of something that is already kuown, that a passage is regarded as descriptive. And as a matter of fact we find thatthe matter dealt with
by the Upanishat passages in question is such as is never cognised
by Sense-perception or the other means of knowledge; and under
the circumstances, how could these passages be regarded as merely descriptive ? How too could they ever stand in need of the

 BENEDICTORY.
eoroboration of any other means of knowledge? Specially as in the
case of tbesepassages, the cognition produced by them is not found
to be necessarily preceded by any other cognition of the same object, as we have in the eise oi' Remembrance (which for this reason
is not regarded as an independent means of knowledge). In fact
it is on this ground that human assertions are regarded as authoritative. These human assertions too do not bring about the
cognition of things, through an indication of the trustworthiness
of the speaker; but they do so independently of the speaker,
depending upon the speaker only for their own appearance (and
not for their faculty of producing cognitions), as the capability
of expressing things is inherent in the word, and inherent
also, in these expressed things, is the capability of being related
to one another, either by mufuil requirement, or by proximity,
or by capability. Consequently, just as in the case of the Veda,
the word is accepted as producing the cognitions of things, independently of any other means of knowledge,—so in-the case of
ordinary human assertions; as, according to the maxim—' ye
laukikd vaidlkästa eva' ('the words of the ordinary human
assertion are the same as those in the Veda'), the potency of
the word must be the same in both cases. As for the inquiry
into the trustworthiness of the speaker, it is simply meant to set
aside the possibility of error with regard to facts ; just as in the
case of Sense-perception also, we look out for the purity and
soundness of the sense-orgao, simply for the sake of setting
aside all doubts as to the erroneous character of the cognition.
We have briefly dealt with this here; for a detailed treatment of the subject, we refer the reader to the Advaynsiddhi.

Reply:—This is not admissible; as in ordinary parlance we
ofcen find a sentence applying to the natural state of things,—
e. <?. the assertion, 'the mango produces good effects, aud the jack
fruit brings undesirable ones.'
Objection:—" In the case of this sentence also, wha-t it does
" is to lay down the eating of the mango, aud the avoiding of
*' the jack fruit, the meaning of the sentence being—' eat the
" mango which produces desirable effects, and avoid the jack fruit
" which leads to evil consequences ' ( hence in this sentence also
" there is no mere description of the natural state of things)"
Reply :—It is not so; as any such laying doion would be
useless; because the man is naturally attached to the eating of
the mango; by the mere cognition of the fact of its producing good
effects ; similarly is he repulsed from the eating of the jack fruit
by the cognition of the fact of its leading to evil consequences.
And as such, wfcutwoul 1 be the necessity of any iujunctionin this
case, where the necessary attraction and repulsion are acomplidhed by tbe nature of the things themselves 1 specially as an injunction has its use only in a case where its object has not been
accomplished by some other means.
Objection:—u The sentence must he regarded as used for the
"purpose of liying down the said attraction and repulsion,^as
" it is with the purpose of such attraction and repulsion that it is
" always found to be used."
Reply:—True ; the sentence does serve the purpose of
attraction and repulsion ; but it does this only as the originator of
these, anreLaot as their (verbal) denoter; artod the evidential authority of words rests only with accomplished things. If, from the
' mere fact of the sentence being used for the purpose of the said attraction and repulsion we were to infer the fact of t>hese two being
verbally denoted by the sentence,—even though they are not

]_ i

cognised as directly expressed by the words,—then, in that case,
even such things as the feeling of satisfaction following on the
eating of the mango, and its digestion, would also have to be
regarded as expressed by the sentence; aod iu the case of Sense«
perception also, when its object would be such as is desired for the
sake of the fulfil ment ofa certain purpose, it would be thisfulfilment
that would have to be regarded as the object of. that sensuous
cognition. As for the fact of the sentence being the originator
of activity, even the Upanisfaxt texts inquestion are such originators; as when one has recognised the true nature of a thing by
means of these, he has recourse to the practice of meditation &c,
which brings about a pure knowledge of the Self, free from ail
doubts and uncertainties; from which knowledge proceeds final
Deliverance. Nor is it necessary that the operation of all
means of knowledge should always end in activity or cessation
from activity; as the3e being dependent upon the wish of the
agent, even when they are not brought about, we have a distinct
perception resting in the thing itself.
Nor is the denotative potency of words restricted to only
such objects as are related to some action ; as we often find words
applying to things not so related; e.g. in the sentence "iha
prabhinnakamalodarerrmdhüni madkukarah pib<tti (withinthis
full blown lotus, the bee is drinking the honey)", which describes
an occurence at the present moment, we rind that one who
knows the meaning of the other words, but does not know that
of the word ' madhükarah', comprehends this word as denoting
that insect which he finds drinking the honey ( and in this case,
the word does not denote anything that is related to an action.)
Objection:—"In this case also, there is au indirect relation"ship with an action; as the person who utters the sentence has
"known the meaning of the word 'madhukarah' only by notici n g tbe actions of older people ".
Reply :—Not so; as there can be no certainty with regard

to this; that is to say, there is no certainty as to whether the
man who utters the sentence had obtained the knowledge of
the meaning of the word, with reference to the object as related
to a certain action of older people, or from its co-extensivness
with otber words knowu to him, or from the direct teaching
(of an older person) with regard to the thing by itself (independently of any action) ; specially as there is no knowing
which of these factors enters first into the comprehension of the
meaning of a word. Then, in accordance with what you hold,
the speaker of the- sentence would have his comprehension with
reference to the object as related to the action, while the hearer
would have it with reference to it as not so related ; and as one
person does not comprehend the meaning of a word by means
of the comprehension of another person, the word 'madhukarak'
would have the two mutually inconsistent characters of having
its denotation related, as well as not related, to an action, as
with reference to the two persons.
Objection :—" The mutual relationship among the meanings of words in a sentence is based upon the requirements of the
verb denoting an action ; and hence there could be no such relationship in the case of the quoted Upaniuhat text which is devoid
of verbs."
Reply :—All Upanishaf texts .are not devoid of verbs ;
an4 even in the case of those that have no verb, there is a
distinct relationship among the things that are denoted by the
words as connected with one another, and are qualified by capability and pro*4mity (to other words).—such relationship being
based upon the mutual requirement of these denotations. For
instance, in the sentence
' känchyclmidänim tribhuvanatilako räjä'—w« are fully cognisant of a connected meaning of
the sentence, though there is no Verb. Or, in such cases the
relationship may be said to be based upon such verbs as 'asti'
or 'bhavati' which may be either distinctly mentioned or only
inferred indirectly.

 PURPOSE OF THE SCIENCE.

This by the way ; to return to the original subject: A collection of the categories is obtained only by means of a due knowledge of the properties of the categories ; as there could be no
collection of the properties \>y themselves alone.
SECTION ( 2 )
PURPOSE OF THE SCIENCE.
Objection :—"A treatise that deals with the properties of
things can never lead to the highest bliss ; as words cannot
accomplish anything besides the denoting of the verbal
meanings."
In reply to this we have the following, wherein it is shown
that a treatise that supplies a knowledge of the properties of
things helps, indirectly, in the fulfilment of the highest end of
man.

പൂർവ്വപക്ഷം: ന്യായഭാഷ്യം, മീമാംസാഭാഷ്യം എന്നിവ നമസ്കാരം കൂടാതെ പൂർണ്ണമായില്ലേ? സിദ്ധാന്തം: അവയിലും നമസ്കാരം ഉണ്ടാകണം — സദ്വൃത്തരായ പക്ഷിലസ്വാമിയും ശബരസ്വാമിയും നമസ്കാരം ഉപേക്ഷിച്ചിരിക്കില്ലെന്നു മ്ലേച്ഛരുപോലും തങ്ങളുടെ ദേവതയെ വന്ദിച്ചല്ലാതെ കാര്യാരംഭം ചെയ്യാത്തതിൽ നിന്നു അനുമേയം.

പദവിഗ്രഹം: 'പ്രണമ്യ' — 'പ്ര' എന്ന ഉപസർഗ്ഗം ഉത്കർഷാർത്ഥം; അതുകൊണ്ടു ദൃഢവിശ്വാസത്തോടും ഭക്തിയോടും കൂടിയ നമസ്കാരം മാത്രമേ പ്രതിബന്ധബീജക്ഷയം വരുത്തി ധർമ്മജനനം ചെയ്യൂ. 'ഹേതും' എന്നതു സർവ്വസൃഷ്ടികളുടെ കാരണൻ ഈശ്വരൻ എന്നു ദ്യോതിപ്പിക്കുന്നു. 'ഈശ്വരം' വിശിഷ്ടദേവതാവിശേഷം. 'മുനിം' — ആത്മജ്ഞാനത്താൽ അജ്ഞാനനാശം പ്രാപിച്ച സർവ്വജ്ഞനായ താപസൻ. 'കണാദം' — വഴിയിൽ വീണ കണങ്ങൾ പെറുക്കിത്തിന്ന് ജീവിച്ച മഹർഷിയുടെ പേർ; 'കണാദശാസ്ത്രം' എന്ന് വ്യപദേശത്തിനു പ്രയോജനമൊന്നുമില്ല, അതുകൊണ്ടു പ്രശസ്തദേവൻ കണാദന്റെ പേർ പറഞ്ഞതു സങ്കല്പമാത്രേണയത്രേ.

ഗ്രന്ഥപ്രയോജനം: 'പദാർത്ഥധർമ്മ' — പദാർത്ഥങ്ങൾ ദ്രവ്യാദി ഷട്, ധർമ്മങ്ങൾ അവയുടെ സാമാന്യവിശേഷലക്ഷണങ്ങൾ. 'പ്രവക്ഷ്യതേ' — കർത്താവ് ഈ ലഘു-സംഗ്രഹം പ്രവചിക്കും. 'മഹോദയം' = മോക്ഷഫലസിദ്ധിജനകം. ഇതുകൊണ്ടു 'പദാർത്ഥജ്ഞാനത്തിനു മനുഷ്യാർത്ഥഫലത്വം ഇല്ല' എന്ന പൂർവ്വപക്ഷം നിരാകൃതം.

മോക്ഷലക്ഷണം: (1) ബൗദ്ധർ — സർവ്വജ്ഞാനനാശം; ഇതു യുക്തമല്ല, ആത്മനാശം ദുഃഖകരം. (2) വേദാന്തികൾ — സർവ്വവാസനാക്ഷയത്തിൽ ശുദ്ധജ്ഞാനോദയം; ഇതും യുക്തമല്ല, ധാരകം ഇല്ലെങ്കിൽ ജ്ഞാനോത്പത്തി ദുരൂഹം. (3) സാംഖ്യർ — പ്രകൃതിയുടെ പ്രവൃത്തിനിവൃത്തിയിൽ പുരുഷാത്മനിഷ്ഠ; ഇതും അയുക്തം, പ്രകൃതി സ്വയം പ്രവൃത്തിമയിയത്രേ. (4) യോഗികൾ — അനന്തസുഖാനുഭവം; ഇതും അനന്തരം നിരാകൃതം. (5) സിദ്ധാന്തം — ദുഃഖത്യന്തനിവൃത്തിയത്രേ മോക്ഷം.

ഉപനിഷദ്വാക്യങ്ങൾ ('അശരീരം വാവ സന്തം ന പ്രിയാപ്രിയേ സ്പൃശതഃ') ദുഃഖനിവൃത്തിയെ സിദ്ധിക്കുന്ന പ്രമാണം. ശബ്ദത്തിന്റെ പ്രമാണത്വം — ലൗകികമെങ്കിലും വൈദികമെങ്കിലും — സ്വതന്ത്രമത്രേ; ഉപനിഷദ്വാക്യങ്ങൾ കാര്യാർത്ഥപരങ്ങളല്ലെങ്കിലും വസ്തുസ്വരൂപപ്രതിപാദകങ്ങളായതുകൊണ്ടു പ്രമാണങ്ങൾ തന്നെ. വിശദമായ വിചാരം 'അദ്വയസിദ്ധി'യിൽ കാണാം.

(തുടർന്ന് പ്രയോജനവിചാരം) വാദി: 'പദാർത്ഥധർമ്മഗ്രന്ഥം മനുഷ്യാർത്ഥസാധനയോഗ്യമല്ല — ശബ്ദത്തിനു അർത്ഥബോധനമല്ലാതെ കാര്യാന്തരം ഇല്ലല്ലോ.' സിദ്ധാന്തി: അടുത്ത ശ്ലോകത്തിലൂടെ (Text 1) ഇതിന്റെ ഉത്തരം — അതായതു പദാർത്ഥജ്ഞാനം പരംഫലത്തിനു പരോക്ഷഹേതുവത്രേ.

en_simple_draft.text:
Śrīdhara opens his commentary by offering his own salutation, first to *Īśvara* — the beginningless, endless, effulgent *kāraṇa* (cause) of the world, whose will is ever-fulfilled and whose body is eternal *caitanya* (pure consciousness) — and then to *Puruṣottama*, the spotless, non-dual Lord seen only by those whose *manas* has reached deep *samādhi* and whose *saṃsāra* has ended.

He then explains why Praśastapāda's opening verse offers *praṇāma* (bow) to *Īśvara* and to *Kaṇāda*. The point is that salutation removes *pratibandha* (obstacles) standing in the way of a work's completion: were it fruitless, no wise person would perform it; if it had any other fruit, it would not be invariably performed at the start of a work; and what is uppermost in mind at that moment is precisely the completion of the work itself.

*Pūrvapakṣa*: But the Nyāya-bhāṣya and the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya were completed without any salutation appearing in them. *Siddhānta*: Those authors — Pakṣila-svāmi and Śabara-svāmi — being good and learned men, must have offered salutation; even *mleccha*s (foreigners) do not begin actions without saluting their own deity.

Word-by-word: *praṇamya* — the prefix *pra* intensifies, so the meaning is intense devoted salutation that creates *dharma* (merit) and destroys the seed of obstacles. *hetum* — without qualification, points to *Īśvara* as cause of all created things. *Īśvaram* — a specific *devatā*. *munim* — an austere ascetic whose ignorance has been destroyed by *ātma-jñāna*. *Kaṇāda* — the sage so called from his having lived on stray *kaṇa* (grains) picked up on the road; the name carries no taint, since the system's excellence is established by its acceptance by great men.

*Padārtha-dharma* — the *padārtha*s are the six categories (*dravya* and the rest); their *dharma*s are their common and specific properties. *pravakṣyate* — "shall be expounded". *mahodayaḥ* — "of great fruit," i.e. *mokṣa*-producing; this answers the objection that a treatise on the properties of categories cannot serve human ends.

Śrīdhara then surveys rival accounts of *mokṣa* (final release) and refutes each: (1) The Bauddha view — cessation of all cognition plus *saṃskāra* — is rejected because annihilation of the Self is not desirable. (2) The Vedāntin view — the rise of *śuddha-jñāna* free of objective taint — is rejected on the ground that *retentiveness* (*saṃskāra*) cannot produce a sharp effect without a permanent substrate. (3) The Sāṃkhya view — *prakṛti*'s cessation upon discrimination — is rejected because *prakṛti*, being inherently active, cannot stop. (4) The Yogi view — eternal unsurpassed pleasure — is set aside for later refutation. (5) The Vaiśeṣika *siddhānta*: *mokṣa* is the absolute cessation of pain (*duḥkha-atyanta-nivṛtti*).

He defends this view with *Upaniṣadic* testimony ("For the bodiless, *priya* and *apriya* do not touch") and a long defence of the *prāmāṇya* (authority) of *śabda* (testimony) — including testimony that describes states rather than enjoins actions, against the Mīmāṃsaka claim that words have authority only for what is to be accomplished. He refers the reader to his *Advayasiddhi* for the full discussion.

He closes the benediction-section by introducing the next move: an objector says "A treatise on the properties of things can never produce the highest good, since words do nothing beyond denoting their objects"; and the reply will come in the next mūla, Text 1.

The 'nature' of a thing is that which constitutes its character. 'Similarity' consists in properties common to many things ;
'Dissimilarity' consists in the property peculiar to a certain
thing. The knowledge leading to the highest result is that of
the true nature (of the six categories) as manifested through
their similarities and dissimilarities.
The pleasure born of the experiencing of sensuous objects
disappears in a moment, and abounds in pain ; and even when
enjoyed in Heaven and such other places it is not lasting, and is
subject to varying grades; for instance, some people enjoy the
pleasures of heaven alone, others enjoy those of the Kingdom of
Heaven. Consequently even this pleasure,—mixed as it is with a

"The theory that Deliverance consists in the cessation of a

Nor can such delirerance be deemed to be desirable for
man; as the cessation of ail pain is the highest end that can be

ml_draft.text:
ഈ പാഠത്തിന്റെ വ്യാഖ്യാനത്തിൽ ശ്രീധരൻ പ്രധാന പദങ്ങളെ വ്യാഖ്യാനിക്കുന്നു. 'തത്ത്വം' — വസ്തുവിന്റെ സ്വരൂപമത്രേ. 'സാധർമ്മ്യം' — അനേകവസ്തുക്കളിൽ ഉള്ള സാമാന്യധർമ്മം. 'വൈധർമ്മ്യം' — ഒരു വസ്തുവിന്റെ മാത്രമുള്ള അസാധാരണധർമ്മം. ഷട്പദാർത്ഥങ്ങളുടെ സാധർമ്മ്യവൈധർമ്മ്യങ്ങളിലൂടെയുള്ള തത്ത്വജ്ഞാനമത്രേ നിശ്രേയസത്തിന്റെ — പരമോത്കൃഷ്ടഫലത്തിന്റെ — സാധനം.

സാംസാരികമായ ഇന്ദ്രിയസുഖങ്ങൾ ക്ഷണികങ്ങളും ദുഃഖമിശ്രങ്ങളുമത്രേ; സ്വർഗ്ഗാദിസ്ഥാനങ്ങളിലെ സുഖവും ശാശ്വതമല്ല, പതനഭയം, ഇതരന്റെ ഉത്കർഷം കാണുമ്പോഴുള്ള മാത്സര്യദുഃഖം എന്നിവയോട് സമ്മിശ്രമത്രേ. അതുകൊണ്ടു സാംസാരികസുഖം 'നിശ്രേയസം' (പരമമംഗളം) അല്ല. ദുരസഹദുഃഖങ്ങളെല്ലാം നിശ്ശേഷം നശിച്ച്, പുനരാവൃത്തി ഇല്ലാത്ത അവസ്ഥയത്രേ ശരിയായ നിശ്രേയസം — അതുതന്നെ പദാർത്ഥതത്ത്വജ്ഞാനത്താൽ പ്രാപ്യം.

മണ്ഡനമിശ്രമതം: 'വിശേഷഗുണനിവൃത്തിയാണ് മോക്ഷം എന്ന വാദം ആത്മനാശത്തിന്റെ വാദത്തിൽ നിന്നു വ്യത്യാസമല്ല.' ഇതിനു ഉത്തരം: ഗുണനിവൃത്തി ആത്മാവിനെ സ്വരൂപപ്രതിഷ്ഠിതമാക്കുന്നു — നിത്യാത്മാവിന്റെ നാശമല്ല ഇതു. ദുഃഖനിവൃത്തി തന്നെ പുരുഷാർത്ഥം.

പൂർവ്വപക്ഷം: 'നിങ്ങളുടെ മോക്ഷം സുഖരഹിതമത്രേ, അതുകൊണ്ടു ഇഷ്ടമല്ല.' സിദ്ധാന്തം: സാംസാരികസുഖവും ദുഃഖമയമത്രേ — ക്ഷണികമാകയാൽ, വിരുദ്ധശക്തികളാൽ ബാധിതമാകയാൽ, സാമഗ്രീസമ്പാദനത്തിന്റെ ക്ലേശം നിമിത്തവുമത്രേ. വിഷം മധുവിൽ ചേർന്നതുപോലെ.

സമാസവിഗ്രഹം: 'ദ്രവ്യഗുണാദി' സൂത്രത്തിലെ പ്രത്യേക ഉദ്ദേശാനുസാരം ദ്വന്ദ്വസമാസമത്രേ. ദ്രവ്യം മുമ്പേ — ഇതരപദാർത്ഥങ്ങളുടെ ആധാരത്വം നിമിത്തം. ഗുണം പിന്നെ — കർമ്മത്തെക്കാൾ സംഖ്യാധിക്യം നിമിത്തം. കർമ്മം ഗുണാനന്തരം — ഗുണാനുവൃത്തി നിമിത്തം. സാമാന്യം കർമ്മാനന്തരം. സമവായം എല്ലാറ്റിലും അന്തർവർത്തിയാകയാൽ ഒടുവിൽ; വിശേഷം സമവായത്തിനു മുൻപു. അഭാവം പ്രത്യേകം ഇല്ല — ഭാവത്തെ ആശ്രയിച്ചതുകൊണ്ടു, അല്ലാതെ പദാർത്ഥമല്ലെന്നല്ല.

en_simple_draft.text:
Śrīdhara unpacks the opening *mūla*. He first glosses the key terms: *tattva* (true nature) is the very *svarūpa* of a thing; *sādharmya* is the *dharma* shared among many things; *vaidharmya* is the *dharma* peculiar to a single thing. Knowing the *tattva* of the six *padārtha*s through these shared and distinguishing features is what produces the highest result.

What is that result? Worldly pleasure — even heavenly pleasure — is fleeting, mixed with dread of falling away, and stained by the heart-burn of seeing another enjoy a higher rank. So it cannot be *niḥśreyasa* ("highest good"). Only the absolute cessation of pain, with no possibility of return, deserves the name; and this is brought about by knowledge of *dravya* and the other categories.

Śrīdhara then refutes Maṇḍana Miśra's barb that defining *mokṣa* as the cessation of a particular *guṇa* (quality, here *duḥkha*) is no different from defining it as annihilation. The reply: the cessation of *duḥkha* allows the *ātman* to rest in its own *svarūpa* and does not destroy the eternal *ātman*. The *pūrvapakṣa* that such a *mokṣa* must be undesirable because it lacks pleasure is met with the observation that worldly *sukha* is itself painful — fleeting, costly to procure, and contradicted by its own counter-forces; it is honey laced with poison.

Śrīdhara then justifies the order of the categories in the compound *dravya-guṇa-karma-sāmānya-viśeṣa-samavāya*: *dravya* leads because all the others rest in it; *guṇa* follows because it outnumbers *karma*; *karma* follows *guṇa* because action travels in the wake of quality; *sāmānya* follows because it relates to *karma*; *viśeṣa* precedes *samavāya* because *samavāya* inheres in all five and so comes last. *Abhāva* is not enumerated separately because it depends conceptually on *bhāva* — not because it is denied categorial status.

Objection:—"If the knowledge of truth be the means of final
beatitude, then dharma could not be the means of it; and this
would involve a contradiction of the sütra, wherein it is declared
that dhtirma is that which leads to final beatitude."
It is in reply to this objection that we have the present text.
The sense of this is that the said beatitude results from dkarma
alone; the knowledge of Substance and the rest beiug regarded as
the means to it, only in so much as such knowledge brings abont
dharma. That is to say, when ail objects, internal and external,
have been duly known, the man comes to notice the evils connected with them and hence acquires an aversion to them; his
desire for such things having thus ceased, the man who has
obtained a knowledge of the self ceases to perform action'«for
the acquiring of those objects, and betakes himself, without any
desire for results, to the practice of those means that are laid
down in the scriptures as calculated to bring about the due renunciation of those objects; and continuing the due practice
of self-knowledge, he accumulates an excellent dharma conducive
to the said renunciation; and the self-knowledge being thereby
fully accomplished, it becomes possible for him to be severed,
absolutely and permanently, from the shackles of the body.
Even in ordinary life we find worldly people renouncing or avoiding such uudesiralile things as a serpent, a thorn and the like,—
such avoidauce resulting from an effort on his part, which is due toa
determination arising from the recognition of the evils following
from those things. In the same manner, the absolute renunciation
of the body &c. can proceed only from a similar property of the self \
(i. e. its efforts) arising from a determination resulting from J
the person's recognition of the evils attendant upon those things.

പൂർവ്വപക്ഷം: 'തത്ത്വജ്ഞാനം മോക്ഷഹേതുവെങ്കിൽ, ധർമ്മം മോക്ഷഹേതുവല്ലെന്നു വരും; ഇതു സൂത്രവിരോധം — സൂത്രത്തിൽ ധർമ്മത്തിന്റെ ഫലമത്രേ നിശ്രേയസമെന്നുണ്ടല്ലോ.' ഉത്തരം: നിശ്രേയസം ധർമ്മത്തിൽ നിന്നു മാത്രമേ ഉണ്ടാകുന്നുള്ളൂ; പദാർത്ഥജ്ഞാനത്തെ മോക്ഷഹേതുവായി പറയുന്നതു — ജ്ഞാനം ധർമ്മത്തെ ജനിപ്പിക്കുന്നതുകൊണ്ടു മാത്രം.

സർവ്വാന്തർബാഹ്യപദാർത്ഥങ്ങളെ അറിയുമ്പോൾ അവയിലെ ദോഷങ്ങളെ കണ്ടു അവയിൽ വൈരാഗ്യം ഉണ്ടാകുന്നു. വൈരാഗ്യത്താൽ വിഷയാർജ്ജനപ്രവൃത്തി നിലയ്ക്കുന്നു; ഫലേച്ഛയില്ലാതെ ശാസ്ത്രവിഹിതങ്ങളായ സന്ന്യാസാദിസാധനങ്ങളിൽ ലയം പ്രാപിക്കുന്നു; വൈരാഗ്യാനുകൂലമായ ഉത്കൃഷ്ടധർമ്മം സഞ്ചയിക്കുന്നു; ആത്മജ്ഞാനം പൂർണ്ണമായാൽ ശരീരാദിബന്ധനങ്ങളിൽ നിന്നു അത്യന്തവിമോചനം പ്രാപ്യമാകുന്നു.

ലൗകികദൃഷ്ടാന്തം: സർപ്പം, മുള്ളു മുതലായ അനിഷ്ടവസ്തുക്കളെ ജനങ്ങൾ — അവയിലെ ദോഷം അറിയുമ്പോൾ — പരിത്യജിക്കുന്നു. അതുപോലെ ശരീരാദിയിലെ ദോഷം അറിയുമ്പോൾ അവയിലെ ത്യാഗപ്രവൃത്തി പ്രയത്നരൂപമായി ആത്മാവിൽ ഉണ്ടാകുന്നു.

ധർമ്മത്തിനു സ്വയം മോക്ഷഹേതുത്വം ഇല്ല — ഈശ്വരേച്ഛയാൽ അഭിവ്യക്തമാകുമ്പോൾ മാത്രമേ ഫലപ്രദമാകുന്നുള്ളൂ. 'ചോദന' — പ്രവർത്തിപ്പിക്കുന്നതു. 'ഈശ്വരചോദന' — ഈശ്വരന്റെ ഇച്ഛാവിശേഷം. 'അഭിവ്യക്തി' — ഫലസിദ്ധിക്കു അഭിമുഖമാകൽ. അതുകൊണ്ടു സൂത്രാർത്ഥം: ഈശ്വരേച്ഛയാൽ ഫലാഭിമുഖമായ ധർമ്മത്തിൽ നിന്നു മാത്രമേ നിശ്രേയസം. 'ച' കാരത്താൽ — സാധർമ്മ്യാദിജ്ഞാനവും ഈ ധർമ്മവും കൂടി മോക്ഷഹേതുവത്രേ എന്നു ദ്യോതിതം.

en_simple_draft.text:
*Pūrvapakṣa*: If the knowledge of *tattva* is the means of *mokṣa*, then *dharma* would not be the means — contradicting the Vaiśeṣika-*sūtra* that names *dharma* as the source of *niḥśreyasa*. *Siddhānta*: *Niḥśreyasa* arises only from *dharma*; the knowledge of the categories is its means only insofar as such knowledge generates the relevant *dharma*.

Once a person has truly known the inner and outer *padārtha*s and seen the *doṣa*s clinging to them, *vairāgya* (dispassion) arises; striving for those objects ceases; he turns, without further desire for results, to the scripture-prescribed means of *sannyāsa*; he accumulates an excellent *dharma* favourable to renunciation; *ātma-jñāna* fully matures; and finally the *bandha* of body and the rest is permanently severed. Even in ordinary life people avoid a snake or a thorn once they have recognised its evils — *prayatna* (effort) following on *niścaya* (determination); the *ātman*'s release from the body works in the same way, but driven by knowledge of the *doṣa*s in *saṃsāra* itself.

But *dharma* by itself is not enough. It must be activated by *īśvara-codanā* — God's particular wish, his commanding will. *codanā* is what urges things to their proper function; *abhivyakti* is the turning of *dharma* toward fruition. The text means: *niḥśreyasa* issues only from the *dharma* that is brought to fruition by the Lord's wish. The particle *ca* indicates that this *dharma* together with the knowledge of *sādharmya* and *vaidharmya* jointly cause final release. (The *Kiraṇāvalī* takes *īśvara-codanā* as a designation for the *Veda*, which the Naiyāyika and Vaiśeṣika regard as God's work, not as a Mīmāṃsaka-style eternal independent entity.)
